units.translation: Foreign to these anapaests is the Doric form Ἀτρειδᾶν [of the Atreidae], whose origin seems to be traced back to the fact that Aeschylus had used the dual number ζεῦγος ζεῦγος Ἀτρείδαιν [a pair, a pair of Atreidae], perhaps mindful of the Homeric Ἀτρείδα δὲ μάλιστα δύω, κοσμήτορε λαῶν [the two Atreidae especially, marshals of the people]. When this was easily mistaken for ΑΤΡΕΙΔΑN, the scribe wrote Ατρειδᾶν [of the Atreidae]. The oldest example of this error is in Homer Il. 19, 310, where some manuscripts, among them the Venetian A, have δοιώ δ᾽ Ἀτρείδαι μενέτην καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς [the two Atreidae remained and godlike Odysseus], but the poet had written what is in others, Ἀτρείδα [the two Atreidae], as the duals dοιώ [two] and μενέτην [they two remained] require, and it is preserved in other places, such as Il. 1, 16. 385 Ἀτρείδα δὲ μάλιστα δύω, κοσμήτορε λαῶν [the two Atreidae especially, marshals of the people], from which it does not follow, as Heynius thought, that in the same place v. 17 Ἀτρεῖδαί τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί [the Atreidae and the other well-greaved Achaeans], or 8, 261 τὸν δὲ μέτ᾽ Ἀτρεῖδαι, Ἀγαμέμνων καὶ Μενέλαος, | τοῖσι δ᾽ ἐπ᾿ Αἴαντες [after them the Atreidae, Agamemnon and Menelaus, and after them the Aiantes], etc., one should write Ἀτρείδα [the two Atreidae]. For when no other dual noun is added, the plural is no less correct than 9, 341 ἢ μούνοι φιλέουσ᾽ ἀλόχους μερόπων ἀνθρώπων | Ἀτρείδαι [or do the Atreidae alone love the wives of mortal men], or Aἴαντες [the Aiantes] in the passage just mentioned, although elsewhere he said Αἴαντε δύω [the two Aiantes]. In a different way there is an error in Photius p. 52, 20 ζεῦγος: τὸ ἐκ δυοῖν τινῶν ζευγνύμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἐκ πλειόνων · καὶ γὰρ καὶ Ἰσοκράτης “τεθρίππων ζεῦγος” εἶπεν καὶ Αἰσχύλος “ζεῦγος τεθρίππων [a yoke: that which is yoked from two things, but also from more; for Isocrates said "a yoke of four-horse chariots" and Aeschylus "a yoke of four-horse chariots"].” The name of Aeschylus is omitted in Etym. M. p. 409, 48. But correctly ζεῦγος τέθριππον [a four-horse yoke] in

Lexicon Vindobonense p. 95, 10, where see Nauck and in the Preface p. XLVIII. To Isocrates p. 351c, where now ἵππων ζεύγει [a pair of horses] is read, Naberus restored τεθρίππῳ [a four-horse chariot].

With the oblique cases Διός [of Zeus], Διί [to Zeus], Δία [Zeus] and the poetic forms Ζηνός [of Zeus], Ζηνί [to Zeus], Ζῆνα [Zeus], which the tragedians do not use unless the meter demands it.
where one should write Ζηνὶ δεσπόσειν τινά [that someone will be lord for Zeus], as I showed under δεσπόζω [to be lord].
Ζηνός [of Zeus] is to be restored for Διός [of Zeus] when the meter demands it.
